The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar ended this practice because, in his view, the reason behind the rule no longer existed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The rule had originally served the need to strengthen and support the Islamic movement during its early weakness. By ʿUmar’s time, Islam had become strong, so the original reason for the rule had disappeared.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The reasoning behind ʿUmar’s decision is important.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It shows Arab thought beginning to extract general principles from legal texts and to adjust particular rulings when the reasons behind them changed along with new needs and new social conditions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We can see the same development among the Companions who spread through the new garrison towns and took on responsibilities in the courts, administration, and military leadership.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Throughout the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, they increasingly used ijtihād based on reasoned opinion.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Eventually, disagreements appeared between the judgments reached by different Companions. These disagreements became serious enough that complaints were made to the caliphs about conflicting legal interpretations.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In general, recording this development in ijtihād gives us an early sign of movement within Arab thought.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

It allows us to follow that development after the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, when this kind of reasoning moved beyond strictly legal questions and began to enter discussion of the beliefs of religion itself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

During the Prophet’s lifetime, the situation had been different. He spoke with the authority of revelation, and “a believer could find no way around his judgment.” Any disagreement among Muslims could be settled by referring the matter back to the Messenger of God.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Here we should return to the disagreements that appeared immediately after the Prophet’s death over the question of the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Each side defended its position through its own form of ijtihād—either by reasoning about the office of the caliphate itself or by interpreting statements and actions attributed to the Prophet in ways that supported its own aims.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

These disagreements continued throughout the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs whenever different interests, political positions, and opinions came into conflict over the organization of the conquests, the administration of the conquered lands, or the courts.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They also reappeared whenever one caliph died and another took his place.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the disagreement did not develop into fully formed schools of thought in the theoretical sense until the end of the Rightly Guided period and the beginning of Umayyad rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
More precisely, this development began during the caliphate of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and the armed conflicts between his supporters and the Umayyads.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Out of these conflicts emerged the Khārijite movement.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Khārijites created theoretical principles of their own. They drew these principles not only from the rules of Islamic law but, more importantly, from basic religious concepts themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They used ijtihād to derive new meanings from those concepts in ways shaped by the position they had taken during the Battle of Ṣiffīn between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We will return to this later.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

For now, we can conclude that the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, especially because of the new conditions created by the conquests, saw Arab thought take noticeable steps toward dealing with new questions and problems through a somewhat freer use of reason.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This development was not limited to legal matters. It also began to touch some questions connected with religious belief itself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

We should now notice that these developments in law and rational reflection were among the first signs that social and cultural interaction between the Arabs and the peoples of their vast state had already begun.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
E — The First Social Revolution in Islam
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We describe the uprising during the reign of the third caliph, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, as the first social revolution in Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In saying this, we have not forgotten the earlier movement of apostasy that led to the Ridda Wars.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But there is an important difference between the two “revolutions,” and this is why we describe the uprising against ʿUthmān as the first of its kind in Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The apostasy movement, although it was produced by social forces that we discussed elsewhere in this chapter, had the character of a counter-revolution against Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The uprising against ʿUthmān was different.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It remained within Islam. In fact, the rebels armed themselves with Islamic ideas themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They acted out of a desire to see the rules and laws of Islam applied fairly and properly, according to what they understood and believed to be the true spirit of Islamic law.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
For this reason, we see it as the first revolution of its kind within Islam itself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb died in 644 CE.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
By then, he had left a strong personal mark on the institutions of the Islamic “state,” and he deserves much of the credit for laying its practical foundations.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Among the changes associated with him were reforms to taxation and new interpretations of the jizya and kharāj.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He exempted certain people from the jizya, especially those who converted to Islam from other religions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
During his rule, additional taxes and fees also began to be imposed on craft industries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Another well-known feature of his rule was the policy of religious tolerance he followed in the conquered lands.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He also took great care to watch the behavior of the governors he appointed there. When he received reports that a governor had wronged the local population, he dealt with the matter firmly.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At times he removed governors from office and confiscated money or property they had unjustly taken from its owners.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This was the conduct of ʿUmar, who became known in both Islamic and non-Islamic historical writing as “ʿUmar the Just.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But once ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān became caliph after him, new patterns began to appear in the behavior of the provincial governors.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They suggested that ʿUmar’s policy and style of rule were being abandoned, with serious consequences.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
People began to feel that the money collected from the jizya, the kharāj, and other taxes was no longer reaching the state treasury.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Instead, it was flowing to the governors appointed by the third caliph, ʿUthmān.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Most of these men belonged to his own family and clan, the Umayyads.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As a result, large fortunes began to accumulate in the hands of a particular group in Medina, the capital of the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Gradually, a new class of extremely wealthy people emerged there. As this class grew, so did the different forms of luxury and material comfort that surrounded it.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This new change requires us to say something about ʿUthmān himself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He came from the aristocratic upper class of Quraysh—the group that had held supreme power in Mecca before the rise of Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He belonged to the Umayyads, one of the ten main branches of Quraysh and among the richest and most powerful in pre-Islamic Mecca.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They had played a leading role in organizing and controlling Meccan trade, especially the family of Abū Sufyān.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was Abū Sufyān who had led the fierce campaign of persecution and opposition against Muḥammad from the time he first proclaimed Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUthmān himself came from this same Umayyad branch of Quraysh and had been one of its richest men before Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Alongside this class background, there was another factor.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

By the time ʿUthmān became caliph after ʿUmar, he was already an elderly man. He no longer had full control over the direction of government—even if he had wished to resist the course taken by the Umayyad governors he appointed from among his closest relatives.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At the same time, the Arab-Islamic state had expanded enormously.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
How could such a state be governed by a caliph who had taken ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s place while possessing so many qualities that sharply distinguished him from his great predecessor?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It seems that many of the Companions already understood the harmful effect these qualities might have on state policy.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

When those effects began to appear in practice, opposition to ʿUthmān’s policies spread through the different Muslim political groups in Medina, even before anger exploded among ordinary Muslims and working people throughout the provinces.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Naturally, the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib were among the strongest opponents.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They saw ʿUthmān’s rise to the caliphate—and ʿAlī’s exclusion from it for the third time—as yet another injustice.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In their view, the difference between the two men in both personal and Islamic qualifications was enormous.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

They therefore saw the decision not only as an injustice against ʿAlī himself, but also as an injustice against what they believed to be a divine right that had belonged to ʿAlī from the very beginning of the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Umayyad governors appointed by ʿUthmān went further and further in building wealth for themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They did not rely only on the income from taxes already established under earlier laws.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They also imposed new, harsh, and heavy taxes on the population and seized land and property from people in the conquered territories.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In this way, these governors gave the state an increasingly semi-feudal character.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They themselves became major owners of farms, land, and other property.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
To the inhabitants of the provinces, the whole state increasingly appeared to have taken on this new semi-feudal character.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Popular anger therefore grew, spread, and became sharper.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

It was strongest among ordinary people and workers, but it also spread among political groups in Medina, especially those who had lost positions at the beginning of ʿUthmān’s reign or whose ambitions for such positions had been frustrated.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In this way, the causes of the coming explosion gathered both beneath the surface and in open political life.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The result was what later Islamic history called the “Great Fitna,” or the “Fitna of ʿUthmān.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But those who gave it this name were not concerned with understanding its historical and social meaning.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That is why they chose a term that, in our view, conceals its real nature.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The true meaning of this explosion lies in the fact that it arose from ordinary people, Arab and non-Arab alike.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

And, as we have said, they wanted Islam to survive and prevail in the same spirit that had originally drawn them to it: a spirit of social change aimed at improving their material conditions and reducing the growing gap between them and the upper groups that were becoming richer at their expense.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

No historian of Islam accused those who came from Egypt and Iraq in 656, as believing pilgrims on their way to Mecca, of rebelling against Islam or preparing a counter-revolution against the Islamic state.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

On the contrary, the historians confirm that these people came to perform the pilgrimage while carrying with them both their belief in Islam and their anger toward those who oppressed them, seized their livelihoods, and accumulated wealth in Islam’s name.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They came to complain to the caliph, ʿUthmān, about the behavior of his relatives who governed in his name.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They then asked him to step down from the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They did not make this demand because they personally hated him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

They believed his resignation was the only solution to the problem facing the people of the provinces: the caliph was unable to control the actions of his relatives, who ruled those provinces in his name.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The representatives of the provinces were then unable to restrain either their own anger or the anger of the ordinary people who had sent them with this demand.
